method_card.title: Cumulative Frequency and Box Plots
method_card.content:
Cumulative frequency is a running total of frequencies. To build a cumulative frequency table, add each frequency to the running total. The final cumulative frequency must equal the total number of values.

When plotting a cumulative frequency curve, plot each cumulative frequency against the upper boundary of its class (not the midpoint). Join the points with a smooth S-shaped curve (or straight lines for a cumulative frequency polygon). The curve always starts at (lower boundary of first class, 0).

For discrete data, a cumulative frequency step polygon is used: the frequency jumps at each exact value rather than being spread across an interval.

Reading off the curve to find quartiles: the median is at the \(\frac{n}{2}\)th value, Q1 is at the \(\frac{n}{4}\)th value, and Q3 is at the \(\frac{3n}{4}\)th value. Draw a horizontal line from the appropriate cumulative frequency, read across to the curve, then drop down to the x-axis.

The interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1. It measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is less affected by extreme values than the full range.

A box plot (box-and-whisker diagram) shows five values: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box spans Q1 to Q3; the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum (or to fences if outliers are excluded at Higher tier). When comparing two box plots, always state a numerical comparison of medians and a numerical comparison of spreads (range or IQR), then interpret both in context.
steps: Build the cumulative frequency column by running total
Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary
Join with a smooth curve (or step polygon for discrete data)
Read the median at n/2, Q1 at n/4, Q3 at 3n/4 from the curve
For box plot comparison: state median comparison AND spread comparison, both in context

exam_context.marks: 3–6 marks; reading median/Q1/Q3 from a given curve is 3 marks; comparing two box plots in context is 3–4 marks
exam_context.frequency: Cumulative frequency curves and box plot comparison appear on almost every paper; the IQR calculation and context comparison are the most-tested Higher extensions

worked_examples.question: A cumulative frequency curve shows data for 40 values. At what cumulative frequency should you read to find the median?

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Draw a horizontal line from cumulative frequency = 20 to the curve, then drop down to find the median.

worked_examples.question: The cumulative frequency curve below shows the masses of 60 parcels. Estimate the median mass.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find the median position
steps.content: Median is at the \(\frac{60}{2} = 30\)th value. Reading across at cf = 30 on the curve, the mass is approximately 11.7 kg.

steps.label: Step 2 — Read from the curve
steps.content: The cf passes 30 in the class 10–15 kg. By interpolation: 23 values ≤10 kg, need the 7th of the 21 in the 10–15 class. Value ≈ \(10 + \frac{7}{21} \times 5 \approx 11.7\) kg.

worked_examples.question: The two box plots below show waiting times at two call centres. Compare the two distributions fully in context.

steps.label: Step 1 — Compare medians
steps.content: Centre A median = 14 min; Centre B median = 10 min. Centre B has shorter typical waiting times by 4 minutes.

steps.label: Step 2 — Compare spread (IQR)
steps.content: Centre A IQR = 22 − 8 = 14 min. Centre B IQR = 16 − 5 = 11 min. Centre B's waiting times are more consistent (smaller IQR).

steps.label: Step 3 — Interpret in context
steps.content: Centre B provides shorter waits on average and more predictable service. Centre A has longer and more variable waiting times.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Centre B has a lower median (10 vs 14 min) and a smaller IQR (11 vs 14 min): it is both faster and more consistent for callers.

bronze.display: A cumulative frequency table shows 80 values. At what cumulative frequency do you read to find Q1?

misconceptions.message: Q1 is at the n/4 position: 80/4 = 20. Don't use n/4 + 1 or 3n/4.

What is the cumulative frequency at ≤30?

misconceptions.message: Read the cumulative frequency directly from the table: at ≤30 it is 34. This is a running total, not the class frequency.

bronze.display: The box plot below shows exam scores. What is the IQR?

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 35 − 15 = 20. Do not confuse IQR with the full range.

bronze.display: A cumulative frequency curve reaches a maximum of 60. At what cumulative frequency position is Q3?

misconceptions.message: Q3 is at 3n/4 = 3×60/4 = 45. Don't use n/4 or n/2 for Q3.

bronze.display: The box plot below shows exam scores. What is the range?

misconceptions.message: Range = maximum − minimum = 90 − 30 = 60. Don't use Q3 − Q1 for the range.

bronze.display: A box plot has median 25 and IQR 18. If the box is symmetric about the median, what are Q1 and Q3?
When plotting a cumulative frequency curve for grouped continuous data, the points are plotted against which value in each class?
options: The midpoint of the class
The lower class boundary
The upper class boundary
The class frequency

misconceptions.message: Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary. Plotting against the midpoint is correct for a frequency polygon, not a CF curve.

silver.display: The cumulative frequency curve below shows data for 40 values. Estimate the median by reading from the curve.

misconceptions.message: Median at cf=20. The cf reaches 18 at x=30 and 30 at x=40. Median is in class 30–40. 2nd of the 12 values in this class: 30 + (2/12)×10 ≈ 31.7. Accept 30–36.

silver.display: The two box plots below compare Group X and Group Y. Which group has the larger IQR?
options: Group X (IQR = 22)
Group Y (IQR = 26)
Both groups have the same IQR
Cannot tell from the box plots

misconceptions.message: IQR X = 42 − 20 = 22. IQR Y = 48 − 22 = 26. Group Y has the larger IQR, meaning more spread in the middle 50%.

silver.display: A cumulative frequency curve for 60 students has median estimated at 54 and Q3 estimated at 68. At what cumulative frequency value should Q1 be read?

misconceptions.message: Q1 is at cumulative frequency n/4 = 60/4 = 15. Draw a horizontal line from cf = 15 to the curve.

silver.display: The two box plots below show delivery times for two couriers. A manager wants the most consistent courier. Which should they choose?
options: Courier A — lower median means faster on average, which is more consistent
Courier B — smaller IQR means more consistent delivery times despite the higher median
Courier A — lower IQR means more consistent delivery times
Courier B — higher median means more reliable

misconceptions.message: Consistency is measured by spread (IQR). Courier B's IQR = 1 day (smaller) means its times cluster more tightly. Courier A is faster on average but less predictable.

silver.display: The box plot below shows test scores for 44 students. Find the IQR.

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 31 − 12 = 19. Do not include the median in this calculation.

gold.display: The two box plots below show heights (cm) of 80 students in each of two schools. Write a full comparison of the two distributions in context.
options: School B students are taller on average (median 165 vs 162 cm) and slightly more consistent (IQR 12 vs 15 cm for A). On average, School B students are 3 cm taller.
School A students are taller on average and more varied in height.
Both schools have similar median heights; School B has a larger IQR.
School B is taller on average but School A is more consistent (larger IQR means more spread).

misconceptions.message: IQR A = 170 − 155 = 15 cm. IQR B = 172 − 160 = 12 cm. B has higher median (taller) and smaller IQR (more consistent). Both comparisons must include the context and numerical values.

gold.display: The cumulative frequency curve below shows 100 values. Find Q1 and Q3 by reading from the curve.

misconceptions.message: Q1 at cf=25: exactly on the ≤20 boundary, so Q1 ≈ 20. Q3 at cf=75: in class 30–40 (cf 58 to 82). Interpolation: 30 + ((75−58)/24)×10 ≈ 30 + 7.1 ≈ 37. Accept 35–39.

gold.display: The cumulative frequency curve below shows exam scores for 120 students. Q1=38, median=52, Q3=64. The pass mark is 45. Estimate the number of students who passed.

misconceptions.message: Read off the CF curve at score=45 to get the number who scored ≤45. Interpolate between Q1=38 (cf=30) and median=52 (cf=60): cf ≈ 30+((45−38)/(52−38))×30 = 30+15 = 45. Passed = 120 − 45 = 75.

gold.display: The two box plots below show salaries (£000s) at two companies. A job-seeker values consistency over average salary. Which company offers more consistent salaries?
options: Company X — lower minimum salary means less variation at the bottom
Company X — larger range means the data is more spread, which some define as consistent
Company Y — smaller IQR (18 vs 20) and smaller range (42 vs 62) both point to greater consistency
Company Y — higher median automatically means more consistent pay

misconceptions.message: IQR X = 44−24 = 20; IQR Y = 46−28 = 18. Range X = 80−18 = 62; Range Y = 62−20 = 42. Company Y has smaller IQR and smaller range: both measures confirm greater consistency.

A step polygon is drawn for this discrete data. At what y-value does the step rise when x changes from 2 to 3?

misconceptions.message: For a step polygon, the step at x=3 rises to the cumulative frequency up to and including 3 absences: 5+12+14+11 = 42. The y-value after the step at x=3 is 42.

gold.display: The box plot below shows the scores of 100 students. The lower fence is defined as Q1 − 1.5 × IQR. Which value is an outlier?
options: Score of 42 (just below Q1)
Score of 10 (well below the lower fence of 12)
Score of 58 (the median)
Score of 82 (just above Q3)

misconceptions.message: IQR = 72 − 48 = 24. Lower fence = 48 − 1.5×24 = 48 − 36 = 12. Any value below 12 is an outlier. Score 10 is below 12, so it is an outlier. Score 42 is above the lower fence of 12, so it is not.
